title: Degrees of calm
core: All three mean undisturbed — no agitation, no ripple, nothing stirring. They part company over *what* holds the calm and *how much credit* the speaker gives for it. One is a surface nothing ruffles, one is a setting nothing has ever troubled, one is a visible clarity that reads as almost luminous. The scale runs from calm that may be mere inertness up to calm that is a kind of achievement.

words.nuance: The only one in the group that can be an insult. **Placid** rates the surface, not the person behind it — nothing ruffles it, but nothing seems to be happening under it either. Cows are placid; call a colleague placid and you have half-implied there is no weather inside.

Belongs to **places and scenes** first — a village at dusk, a stretch of water, an afternoon. Its claim is historical: nothing ever disturbed this, so there was no storm to recover from. Applied to a person it reports an untroubled life, not composure under fire.

The calm that **shows**, and that holds when it has no business holding — a face unclouded while the room panics. Where **placid** risks vacancy, **serene** implies something is being mastered; hence the near-spiritual, faintly grand air (monks, dawn, *Your Serene Highness*).

exam_note: The GRE leans on **placid**'s pejorative shade — in a sentence criticizing a dull character, "placid" fits where "serene" and "tranquil" (both approving) cannot; and it rewards knowing **serene** is the only one that survives surrounding chaos.
